Empirical Research Plan  
“How do mergers and acquisitions affect markup pricing in the finance sector?”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Chosen design: Difference-in-Differences (DID) with an event-study extension (dynamic DID).

Why this works  
• We observe treated and never-treated firms for 60+ quarters before/after well-timed, publicly announced M&A events.  
• Quarterly panel → rich pre-trends tests and firm & time fixed effects.  
• No obvious running variable with a sharp cutoff, and plausible exogenous timing makes IV or RDD less natural.  
• Event-study coefficients let us (i) test the parallel-trend assumption and (ii) trace post-merger markup dynamics.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
Treated_it = 1 for firm i in all quarters t ≥ q₀ᵢ, where q₀ᵢ is the first quarter whose closing date follows the public announcement of an acquisition in which firm i is the acquirer (primary specification) or the combined entity (robustness).

Control group  
Never-treated firms drawn from the same 2-digit SIC finance subsectors (commercial banks, insurance, brokerage, etc.) that:  
(a) never announce or complete an M&A in the sample window, and  
(b) match treated firms on pre-event size, leverage, and pre-event mark-up level (propensity-score or coarsened-exact matching; we keep all matches with replacement).

Event time  
τ = q – q₀ᵢ, where τ = 0 is the first post-announcement quarter. We keep τ ∈ [-12, +12] (three-year window) for the event-study.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel Trends: Absent an acquisition, treated and control firms would have evolved similarly in markups.  
Plausibility: same industry, matched covariates, and pre-τ leads testable.

A2. No Anticipation: Firms do not change markups materially before the public announcement.  
Plausibility: finance-sector pricing largely contract-based; M&A negotiations are private. Leads test (τ < 0) will reveal violations.

A3. No Spillovers/Stable Unit Treatment (SUTVA): One firm’s merger does not directly alter another non-treated firm’s prices.  
Plausibility: some spillovers (e.g., local competition) possible; we cluster at 2-digit SIC×quarter and run robustness excluding geographic peers.

A4. Exogenous Timing Conditional on Controls: After conditioning on firm FE, industry-time FE, and controls, merger timing is as-good-as-random w.r.t. future markup shocks.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Selection on Parallel Trend Violations  
• Mitigation: event-study leads, pre-trend placebo (fake event dates), matching quality diagnostics, firm-specific linear trends.

T2. Simultaneous Regulatory Shocks (e.g., 1994 Riegle-Neal Act)  
• Mitigation: interact quarter FE with sub-industry and with bank-holding-company dummy; drop windows straddling major regulatory reforms as robustness.

T3. Anticipatory Price Changes & Announcement Leakage  
• Mitigation: include τ = -4 to ‑1 leads; re-define “event” as completion date instead of announcement; measure expectations via abnormal stock returns and control for them.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)       # fast high-dimensional FE regressions
library(MatchIt)      # matching
library(broom)

# 1. Load data
dat <- read_csv("finance_MA_quarterly.csv")   # ──> columns: firm_id, date, qtr, sic2,
                                              # mark_up, announced, completed, assets,
                                              # leverage, stock_ret, ...

# 2. Pre-processing
dat <- dat %>%
  mutate(quarter = as.yearqtr(date),
         treated_firm = if_else(announced == 1, 1, 0)) %>%
  group_by(firm_id) %>%
  mutate(event_q = ifelse(any(treated_firm == 1),
                          min(quarter[treated_firm == 1]),
                          NA)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(event_time = ifelse(!is.na(event_q),
                             as.numeric(quarter - event_q),
                             NA),
         post = ifelse(event_time >= 0 & !is.na(event_time), 1, 0))

# 3. Match treated vs. never-treated firms using pre-event characteristics
pre_event <- dat %>% filter(event_time < 0 | is.na(event_time))
match_data <- pre_event %>% 
  select(firm_id, treated_firm, assets, leverage, mark_up) %>% 
  distinct()

m.out <- matchit(treated_firm ~ log(assets) + leverage + mark_up,
                 data = match_data, method = "nearest", ratio = 2)
matched_ids <- match.data(m.out)$firm_id
dat_matched <- dat %>% filter(firm_id %in% matched_ids)

# 4. Main DID regression
did_est <- feols(mark_up ~ post * treated_firm | firm_id + quarter,
                 data = dat_matched, cluster = ~ firm_id)

summary(did_est)

# 5. Event-study specification
es_est <- feols(mark_up ~ i(event_time, treated_firm, ref = -1) |
                            firm_id + quarter,
                data = dat_matched %>% filter(event_time %in% -12:12),
                cluster = ~ firm_id)
etable(es_est, dict = c("i(event_time,treated_firm, ref=-1)" = "τ"))

# 6. Robustness: add firm-specific trends
did_trend <- feols(mark_up ~ post * treated_firm | firm_id + quarter + 
                                 firm_id:trend,
                   data = dat_matched %>% 
                          mutate(trend = as.numeric(quarter)),
                   cluster = ~ firm_id)
summary(did_trend)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Economic theory (market-power & efficiency):  
• Direction: Positive – mergers in finance likely raise markups by easing price competition.  
• Magnitude: back-of-the-envelope 2–5 pp increase in markups (≈ 5–10% of pre-M&A average), largest in concentrated subsectors (e.g., credit-card issuing).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
(C1) Pre-treatment parallel trends testable and passes: 1  
(C2) No anticipatory effects (lead coefficients near zero): 0.5  
(C3) No spillovers between treated and control units: 0.5  
(C4) Stable composition / no differential attrition: 1  
(C5) Robustness to alternative specifications (trends, matching, placebo): 1  

Total ≈ 4/5 → design reasonably credible but still sensitive to spillovers and anticipation.
